s3_notes: Slide 3: Timeline of 140+ years of tradition (9 milestones). Key focus on Milestone 1 (1882: Founding in Stuttgart – The journey begins with piano actions; parallel to Carl Rönisch), Milestone 2 (1906: Dedicated hammerhead manufacturing – From Cristofori's leather-covered paper roll in 1700 to Renner's proprietary hammerhead production from 1906, which would later define the tone of every Steinway grand and establish a worldwide benchmark; image series featuring Cristofori, 1700 hammer action, historical action manufacturing and 1906 hammerhead presses), Milestone 3 (1911: Modernization & grand action manufacturing – Érard repetition action as cornerstone of modern grand piano playing; transition to Renner's first grand piano actions; Oscar Renner's industrial modernization with cutting-edge machinery, streamlined methods and transition from shaft drives to hundreds of individual electric motors; uniting all branches under one roof; image series featuring Sébastien Érard, 1808 Érard action and electrified workshop), Milestone 4 (1944: Air raid & rebuilding), Milestone 5 (1951/1952: Dr. Manfred Renner; 1955 return), Milestone 6 (1990: Fall of the Wall, historic turning point & survival – acquisition of Piano Union's action facility in Zeitz amidst pressure from Czech competitors to preserve largest customer Schimmel producing >40 pianos/day), Milestone 7 (2011: New facility in Gärtringen and modern manufacturing in Meuselwitz after relocating from Zeitz; consolidation across two core sites: Meuselwitz 6,800 m² and Gärtringen; image series featuring Gärtringen new facility and Meuselwitz bird's-eye view), Milestone 8 (2019: Steinway & Sons acquisition; tribute to Clemens von Arnim) and Milestone 9 (Preserving tradition, shaping future: Full consolidation of all operations in Meuselwitz following October 2025 launch with modern facility and new central filtration & extraction system; gratitude to Gärtringen workforce).

s8_title: Carding: Parallel Alignment into Flowing Fleece

s33_category: Part 5: Voicing • Opening: Piano Tone Physics & Partials
s33_title: Partial Structure on A₁ (55 Hz): Felt Hardness & Strike Point
s33_subtitle: Increase and decrease of partials H₁–H₁₂ in decibels (dB) driven by hammer felt elasticity and strike ratio
s33_str_title: Standing Wave A₁ (1,560 mm) & Node Cancellation
s33_notes: Slide 33 (Chapter 5 Opening: Voicing): Interactively demonstrate on bass note A₁ (55 Hz, speaking length L = 1,560 mm) how a piano tone is built from partials H₁–H₁₂. First show felt hardness: a softer, needled hammer lengthens contact time τc (~3.8 ms) and reduces upper partials in dB, whereas a harder crown (τc ~1.3 ms) boosts upper partials sharply. Next demonstrate the Young-Helmholtz strike-point law: striking near 1/8 L or 1/7 L suppresses dissonant partials (H₇ natural seventh, H₉ major second) at their nodes while preserving the singing major third H₅ (1/5 L).
s34_category: Part 5: Voicing • Spring Physics, Compaction Zones & Dynamic Limits
s34_title: The Hammerhead as a Complex Spring: From Cristofori to Zone Balance
s34_subtitle: How elasticity, 2:1 crown-to-flank compaction, and transition stiffness govern playable dynamics (pp to ff)
s34_curve_title: Change in Partial Structure (H1–H12 in dB)
s34_notes: Start with 1. Cristofori Roll (1700): His leathered hollow parchment cylinder uses circumferential surface tension with zero dead core mass to generate high restoring force and short contact time τc. Then switch to 2. Renner Tension Spring: Peak compaction sits at the crown, dropping to half (½) at the widest flank, while uncut wool fibers taper onto the wood moulding fixed by glue and rivet. Use the 3-stage toggles to show why dynamics are an outcome: an overly hard crown/transition prevents pianissimo, while insufficient elasticity or a stiff outer-contour bridge locks out the flank, prolongs τc, prevents fortissimo, and reshapes partials H1–H12.
